questions.stem: A patient with a ruptured spleen is taken for a laparotomy. His blood pressure is 80/50 and heart rate is 125/min. Induction agent of choice for this patient is?
questions.solutionHtml:
t-family:"Calibri",sans-serif"> This agent typically results in reduced blood pressure by depressing central sympathetic tone, which could be detrimental for a hypotensive patient, risking further cardiovascular compromise.

Option B. Fentanyl: A potent opioid that can lead to further depression of the central nervous system and potentially exacerbate hypotension and reduce heart rate, not ideal under the patient's current circulatory stress.

Option D. Halothane: Known to decrease myocardial contractility and potentially worsen hypotension, Halothane would not be appropriate for someone whose blood pressure is already critically low.

Educational Objective:

Ketamine uniquely preserves and can elevate blood pressure during induction of anesthesia, making it an optimal choice for patients presenting with hypotension.

questions.stem: A perioperative patient was given a skeletal muscle relaxant that acts by competitive inhibition of nicotinic ACh receptors. What agent can be used for the reversal of its effects?​​​
questions.solutionHtml:
ont-family:Aptos,sans-serif">Option A. Physostigmine: Also a cholinesterase inhibitor but primarily crosses the blood-brain barrier and could cause CNS adverse effects; not typically used for reversing NMBs.

Option C. Succinylcholine: A depolarizing NMB, which is inappropriate for reversal and instead causes muscle relaxation.

Option D. Carbachol: A cholinergic agonist used to treat glaucoma and urinary retention but not for reversing neuromuscular blockade.

Educational Objective:

Understand the use of neostigmine as a reversal agent for non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers by its mechanism of increasing acetylcholine concentration, which competes with the blocker at the nicotinic receptors.

questions.stem: Epinephrine added to a solution of lignocaine for a peripheral nerve block will:

options.label: B
options.text: Increase the duration of action of the local anesthetic

questions.answerText: Increase the duration of action of the local anesthetic
questions.solutionHtml:
span>

 

Option A. Increase risk of convulsions: Incorrect, as epinephrine does not typically increase the risk of convulsions related to local anesthetic use. Instead, by reducing systemic absorption, it might actually help prevent peak plasma levels that could lead to toxicity.

 

Option C. Both A & B: Incorrect, since only B is true.

 

Option D. None of these: Incorrect, as epinephrine does increase the duration of action.

 

Educational Objective:


Adding epinephrine to lignocaine not only enhances the duration of the anesthetic effect but also helps minimize bleeding, making it highly beneficial for longer procedures and areas of significant vascularization.

questions.stem: Which of the following drugs undergoes Hoffman’s elimination?
questions.solutionHtml:
pan style="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Option B. Pancuronium: Does not undergo Hoffman's elimination; it is metabolized by the liver and excreted by the kidneys.

 

Option C. Mivacurium: Is metabolized by plasma cholinesterases, not through Hoffman’s elimination.

 

Option D. Vecuronium: Is primarily metabolized in the liver and excreted by the kidneys, not involving Hoffman's elimination.

 

Educational Objective:


Remember that Atracurium undergoes Hoffman’s elimination, a process allowing safe use in patients with liver and kidney dysfunction, distinguishing it from other neuromuscular blockers that require metabolic clearance by these organs.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman goes to her dermatologist to have a mole removed. The patient tells her physician that she had an allergic reaction to a local anesthetic the last time she had dental work performed. Examination of her dental records by her dentist reveals that the patient received procaine for a tooth extraction. Which of the following drugs would be appropriate for the present procedure?
questions.solutionHtml:
span style="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif"> Incorrect, as it is an ester local anesthetic like procaine.

 

Option B. Chloroprocaine: Incorrect, another ester local anesthetic.

 

Option C. Cocaine: Incorrect, also an ester local anesthetic and has additional significant side effects.

 

Educational Objective:


In patients allergic to ester local anesthetics, amide local anesthetics like mepivacaine are preferred due to their different metabolic pathways, reducing the risk of allergic reactions.

questions.stem: Dantrolene is useful in all except?
questions.solutionHtml:
"> 

Option A. Malignant neuroleptic syndrome: Correct, Dantrolene is used for the treatment of this syndrome, which can cause severe muscle rigidity and elevated temperature similar to malignant hyperthermia.

 

Option C. Malignant hyperthermia: Correct, it is a primary treatment for this condition, which involves a critical rise in body temperature and severe muscle contractions.

 

Option D. Upper motor neuron disorders: Correct, Dantrolene helps manage symptoms of spasticity associated with these disorders.

 

Educational Objective:


Dantrolene is valuable in conditions associated with hyperactivity of skeletal muscle contraction but not in the treatment of malignant hypertension, underscoring the importance of understanding its specific applications related to muscle relaxation and thermal regulation.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old carpenter presents to the ER after an accident in which he inadvertently chopped off the tip of his index finger. He is taken to the OR for reattachment of the digit, and after sedation, a local anesthetic is administered around the site of the injury. The local anesthetic used in the procedure did not contain any epinephrine, as it usually does for most surgical procedures. The reason for this is?

options.label: A
options.text: Epinephrine causes increased blood loss during delicate surgery

options.label: B
options.text: Epinephrine causes swelling of the tissues, making surgery more challenging

options.label: C
options.text: Epinephrine is contraindicated in emergency surgery

options.label: D
options.text: Epinephrine causes vasoconstriction, which can lead to vascular ischemia in digits

questions.answerText: Epinephrine causes vasoconstriction, which can lead to vascular ischemia in digits
questions.solutionHtml:
s,sans-serif">Explanation:

Options A and B. Incorrect because epinephrine actually reduces blood loss and swelling in most surgical areas due to its vasoconstrictive effects.

Option C. Incorrect as epinephrine is not universally contraindicated in emergency surgeries, but its use depends on the specific circumstances and locations involved.

Educational Objective:

Recognize the contraindication of epinephrine in local anesthetics used for surgeries on digits due to the risk of causing vascular ischemia, highlighting the need for careful consideration of vasoconstrictive additives in anesthetics depending on the surgical site.

questions.stem: Centrally acting muscle relaxant with alpha 2 adrenergic agonist activity is:
questions.solutionHtml:
rif">Explanation:

Option A. Chlorzoxazone: Acts primarily by depressing reflexes at the spinal level or possibly within the brain, but its exact mechanism is not well understood and does not involve alpha-2 adrenergic agonism.

Option B. Baclofen: Is a GABA-B receptor agonist that reduces excitatory transmission in the spinal cord, differing from the alpha-2 adrenergic mechanism of Tizanidine.

Option D. Pirenzepine: Is an M1 muscarinic receptor antagonist primarily used to treat peptic ulcer disease, not related to muscle relaxation or alpha-2 adrenergic agonism.

Educational Objective:

Tizanidine's mechanism as an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist centrally reduces spasticity, distinguishing it from other muscle relaxants that may act through different neurotransmitter pathways or receptor types.

questions.stem: A 70 kg young athlete was planned for surgery. during anaesthesia, vecuronium was not available, so repeated doses of succinylcholine was given intermittently up to 640 mg. During recovery, patient was not able to spontaneously respire and move limbs. What is the cause?

options.label: C
options.text: Muscle weakness due to repeated fasciculations

questions.solutionHtml:
font-family:Aptos,sans-serif">Option A. Pseudocholinesterase deficiency: Typically results in prolonged paralysis after the administration of succinylcholine due to decreased enzyme activity needed for its breakdown, but not directly linked to repeated doses.

Option C. Muscle weakness due to repeated fasciculations: While initial fasciculations occur with succinylcholine, they do not usually result in long-term muscle weakness or inability to breathe.

Option D. Undiagnosed muscular dystrophy: Would not likely be revealed by the use of succinylcholine, and muscle weakness would have pre-existed the surgery.

Educational Objective:

Repeated doses of succinylcholine can lead to a phase II blockade, a state where muscles become unresponsive to further neural stimulation despite being repolarized, important to monitor and manage during surgeries requiring prolonged muscle relaxation.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old office worker consults his family physician due to recurring neck and shoulder muscle spasms that have been troubling him for the last month. He mentions that these spasms seem to worsen after long hours of working at his computer. Physical examination shows localized muscle tenderness but no neurological abnormalities. After discussing treatment options and considering the patient's work environment, the physician thinks of prescribing cyclobenzaprine, a commonly used muscle relaxant, to alleviate the patient's symptoms. What is the primary mechanism of action of cyclobenzaprine in the treatment of muscle spasms?

options.label: D
options.text: Acting as a GABA_A receptor agonist

questions.solutionHtml:
n:justify"> 

Option A. Decreasing nerve conduction: Incorrect, as cyclobenzaprine does not primarily work by decreasing overall nerve conduction; it specifically targets polysynaptic reflexes.

 

Option C. Blocking conduction across NM junction: Incorrect, this is characteristic of neuromuscular blocking agents used in anesthesia, not cyclobenzaprine.

 

Option D. Acting as a GABA_A receptor agonist: Incorrect, cyclobenzaprine does not act via GABAergic mechanisms but through a modulation of serotoninergic and noradrenergic pathways.

 

Educational Objective:


Cyclobenzaprine is effective in treating muscle spasms due to its ability to inhibit spinal polysynaptic reflexes, providing symptomatic relief from muscle rigidity and spasms commonly exacerbated by posture and repetitive motion.

questions.stem: Blockade of nerve conduction by a local anesthetic is characterized by?

options.label: A
options.text: Greater potential to block a resting nerve as compared to a stimulated nerve

options.label: B
options.text: Need to cross the cell membrane to produce the block

options.label: C
options.text: Large and myelinated fibers are blocked before the unmyelinated fibers

options.label: D
options.text: Cause consistent change of resting membrane potential

questions.answerText: Need to cross the cell membrane to produce the block
questions.solutionHtml:
amily:Aptos,sans-serif">Explanation:

 

Option A. Greater potential to block a resting nerve as compared to a stimulated nerve: Incorrect, as local anesthetics more effectively block nerves that are frequently active or depolarized.

 

Option C. Large and myelinated fibers are blocked before the unmyelinated fibers: Incorrect. In general, local anesthetics block smaller, unmyelinated fibers before larger, myelinated fibers. This is because smaller fibers have a higher surface area to volume ratio and require less anesthetic to achieve effective blockade. Pain fibers (which are small and often unmyelinated) are typically blocked before motor fibers (which are larger and myelinated).

 

Option D. Cause consistent change of resting membrane potential: Incorrect, local anesthetics do not typically change the resting membrane potential; they block the action potential propagation by inhibiting sodium influx.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Local anesthetics must penetrate the neuronal membrane to effectively block nerve conduction, highlighting the importance of their lipophilic characteristics to cross membranes and achieve their pharmacological effect.

questions.stem: Mechanism of action of centrally acting muscle relaxant:

options.label: A
options.text: Decreases voluntary power and does not paralyze

options.label: B
options.text: Increases voluntary power and does not paralyze

options.label: C
options.text: Decrease muscle tone without reducing voluntary power

options.label: D
options.text: Decreases voluntary power and cause muscle paralysis

questions.answerText: Decrease muscle tone without reducing voluntary power
questions.solutionHtml:
n style="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Option A. Decreases voluntary power and does not paralyze: Incorrect, as these drugs do not typically decrease voluntary power.

 

Option B. Increases voluntary power and does not paralyze: Incorrect, these drugs do not increase voluntary power.

 

Option D. Decreases voluntary power and cause muscle paralysis: Incorrect, centrally acting muscle relaxants do not cause paralysis or decrease voluntary power.

 

Educational Objective:


Centrally acting muscle relaxants are effective in managing spasticity by decreasing muscle tone without compromising voluntary muscle control, ideal for patients with chronic spastic conditions.

Option C. Minimal cardiovascular side-effects: Correct, it has minimal effects on the cardiovascular system, making it suitable for patients with cardiovascular instability.

 

Option D. Low blood solubility: Correct, the low solubility facilitates quick onset and offset of its anesthetic effects, leading to rapid recovery.

Educational Objective:

 

Xenon is Greek for stranger. It is the only noble gas to be anaesthetic under normobaric conditions. Xenon is extremely rare with an average room containing only 4 ml. It is very close to the ‘ideal agent’.

 

Advantages of Xenon Anesthesia

  1. Inert (probably non-toxic to liver and kidney with no metabolism)
  2. Minimal effect on CVS function
  3. Lowest blood solubility (Lowest blood gas partition coefficient) therefore rapid induction and recovery.
  4. Does not trigger malignant hyperthermia
  5. Environment friendly
  6. Non-explosive

 

Disadvantages of Xenon Anesthesia

  1. High cost
  2. Low potency (MAC = 70%)
  3. No commercially available anaesthesia equipment.

questions.stem: Mechanism of action of curare like drugs are:

options.label: B
options.text: Act competitively on Ach receptors blocking post-synaptically

options.label: C
options.text: Repetitive stimulation of Ach receptors on muscle end plate

options.label: D
options.text: Inhibiting the calcium channel on presynaptic membrane

questions.answerText: Act competitively on Ach receptors blocking post-synaptically
questions.solutionHtml:
Option A. Persistently depolarizing at neuromuscular junction: Incorrect, this describes the mechanism of depolarizing blockers like succinylcholine, not curare-like drugs.

 

Option C. Repetitive stimulation of Ach receptors on muscle end plate: Incorrect, curare-like drugs block rather than stimulate these receptors.

 

Option D. Inhibiting the calcium channel on presynaptic membrane: Incorrect, curare-like drugs do not interact with calcium channels in their primary mechanism of action.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Curare-like drugs are non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers that work by competing with acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, effectively preventing muscle contractions necessary for various surgical procedures.

During the surgery, the anesthesiologist notices tall, peaked T waves and prolongation of the PR interval, accompanied by progressive widening of the QRS complex so that it appears to merge with the T waves. The patient goes into ventricular fibrillation, then asystole, and cannot be resuscitated. Which of the following agents is most likely responsible for this patient's electrocardiographic changes?

Option B. Baclofen: Incorrect, it is a centrally acting muscle relaxant used for spasticity and does not cause electrolyte imbalances.

 

Option C. Halothane: Incorrect, it is known for potential risks of hepatotoxicity and malignant hyperthermia but does not typically induce hyperkalemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In patients with extensive burns, succinylcholine should be avoided due to the risk of exacerbating hyperkalemia, which can lead to life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias and cardiac arrest.

questions.stem: Postoperative vomiting is uncommon with this intravenous anaesthetic agent and patient are able to ambulate sooner than those who receive other anaesthetic agents:

Option B. Enflurane: An older inhalation anesthetic associated with longer recovery times and higher incidences of PONV.

 

Option D. Remifentanil: While effective for pain management, it is an opioid and does not inherently reduce PONV or quicken recovery times compared to Propofol.

Propofol is advantageous for its antiemetic properties and its ability to allow patients to ambulate sooner after surgery, which supports its preference in settings that require rapid recovery and minimal postoperative complications. questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true of local anesthetics?

options.label: A
options.text: The local anesthetic is required in the unionized form for penetrating the neuronal membrane.

options.label: B
options.text: The local anesthetic approaches its receptor from the intraneuronal face of the Na+ channel.

options.label: C
options.text: The local anesthetic binds to its receptor mainly when the Na+ channel is in the resting state.

options.label: D
options.text: The local anesthetic combines with its receptor in the ionized cationic form.

questions.answerText: The local anesthetic binds to its receptor mainly when the Na+ channel is in the resting state.
questions.solutionHtml:
n>

 

Option A. The local anesthetic is required in the unionized form for penetrating the neuronal membrane: True, as the unionized form is more lipophilic and can cross lipid membranes more easily.

 

Option B. The local anesthetic approaches its receptor from the intraneuronal face of the Na+ channel: True, once inside the neuron, the local anesthetic can access and bind to the inner portion of the sodium channel.

 

Option D. The local anesthetic combines with its receptor in the ionized cationic form: True, the ionized form of the drug is the active form that interacts with the sodium channel to block nerve conduction.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Understanding the dual nature of local anesthetics' interaction with sodium channels is crucial. They must be capable of both lipophilic and hydrophilic behavior to effectively penetrate nerve cells and exert their blocking action, highlighting the importance of their molecular structure in clinical efficacy.

questions.stem: Cardiac or central nervous system toxicity may result when standard lignocaine doses are administered to patients with circulatory failure. This may be due to the following reason?

options.label: A
options.text: Lignocaine concentration is initially higher in relatively well perfused tissues such as brain and heart

options.label: B
options.text: Histamine receptors in brain and heart get suddenly activated in circulatory failure

options.label: C
options.text: There is a sudden outburst of release of adrenaline, noradrenaline and dopamine in brain and heart

options.label: D
options.text: Lignocaine is converted to a toxic metabolite due to its longer stay in the liver

questions.answerText: Lignocaine concentration is initially higher in relatively well perfused tissues such as brain and heart
questions.solutionHtml:
"text-align:justify"> 

Option B. Histamine receptors in brain and heart get suddenly activated in circulatory failure: This is incorrect as histamine receptor activation is not directly related to lignocaine's mechanism of action nor its distribution.

 

Option C. There is a sudden outburst of release of adrenaline, noradrenaline, and dopamine in brain and heart: While stress hormones do increase in circulatory failure, this does not directly affect the pharmacokinetics or local concentrations of lignocaine.

 

Option D. Lignocaine is converted to a toxic metabolite due to its longer stay in the liver: Incorrect, as lignocaine is indeed metabolized in the liver, but its metabolites are generally not significantly toxic, and the primary concern in circulatory failure is not hepatic metabolism but altered tissue distribution.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In circulatory failure, increased lignocaine concentrations in well-perfused organs such as the brain and heart can lead to toxicity, highlighting the need for cautious dosing and monitoring in patients with compromised circulation.

questions.stem: All the following statements about lignocaine are true except:

options.label: A
options.text: It blocks active sodium channels with more affinity than resting sodium channels

options.label: C
options.text: It is given orally for treatment of cardiac arrhythmias

options.label: D
options.text: Adrenaline increases the duration of action of lignocaine when used for infiltration anaesthesia

questions.answerText: It is given orally for treatment of cardiac arrhythmias
questions.solutionHtml:
p style="text-align:justify">Explanation:

Option A. It blocks active sodium channels with more affinity than resting sodium channels: True, lignocaine preferentially binds to and blocks sodium channels in their active or open state, which contributes to its effectiveness as a local anesthetic.

Option B. It can cause cardiotoxicity: True, at high blood concentrations, lignocaine can have toxic effects on the heart, including arrhythmias and cardiac arrest.

Option D. Adrenaline increases the duration of action of lignocaine when used for infiltration anesthesia: True, adrenaline (epinephrine) is added to lignocaine in infiltration anesthesia to cause vasoconstriction, which reduces blood flow and slows the absorption of lignocaine, thereby prolonging its duration of action and reducing systemic toxicity.

Educational Objective:

Understand that lignocaine is ineffective orally for cardiac arrhythmias due to its high first-pass metabolism, necessitating intravenous administration for therapeutic effectiveness.



erentially binds to and blocks sodium channels in their active or open state, which contributes to its effectiveness as a local anesthetic.

questions.stem: d-Tubocurarine acts by?

options.label: A
options.text: Inhibiting nicotinic receptors at myoneural junction

options.label: B
options.text: Inhibiting nicotinic receptors at autonomic ganglion

questions.answerText: Inhibiting nicotinic receptors at myoneural junction
questions.solutionHtml:
">Option B. Inhibiting nicotinic receptors at autonomic ganglion: Incorrect, as d-Tubocurarine specifically targets nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction, not autonomic ganglia.

Option C. Producing depolarizing block: Incorrect, d-Tubocurarine is a non-depolarizing blocker, unlike succinylcholine, which produces a depolarizing block.

Option D. By inhibiting reuptake of acetylcholine: Incorrect, d-Tubocurarine does not affect the reuptake of acetylcholine; it competes with acetylcholine at the receptor level.

Educational Objective:

Recognize d-Tubocurarine as a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that inhibits nicotinic receptors at the myoneural junction, used primarily to induce muscle relaxation during surgery.
